Several 3d metals release more energy on gaining an electron than nearby p-block elements. Copper's added electron completes its 4s pair (3d10 4s2) and nickel's nearly fills its 3d subshell, so both outscore the group 13 elements and even phosphorus, arsenic and germanium; vanadium, chromium and cobalt also outscore the group 13 elements, whose added p electron is weakly held.

A group 13 atom's added electron goes into a p orbital shielded by the filled s pair beneath it, so it is held weakly, while an alkali metal's added electron completes its s pair. The alkali metal releases slightly more energy, against the across-period rule.

Group 15 atoms have a half-filled p subshell, so an added electron must pair up in an occupied orbital, which costs repulsion energy. That keeps their electron affinities below group 14's, and because the pairing cost is smaller in larger atoms, the values rise rather than fall going down the group.
